title: Part 2, Chapter 7
paragraphs: An elegant carriage stood in the middle of the road, drawn by a pair of spirited grey horses. There was no one inside, and the coachman had climbed down from his seat. The horses were being held by the bridle.... A mass of people had gathered, with the police in front. One officer held a lighted lantern, turning it on something lying near the wheels. Everyone was talking, shouting, exclaiming. The coachman seemed at a loss and kept repeating:
"What a disaster! Good Lord, what a disaster!"

Raskolnikov pushed his way in and finally managed to see what was causing the commotion. On the ground lay a man who had been run over, apparently unconscious and covered in blood. He was very poorly dressed, but not like a laborer. Blood poured from his head and face. His face was crushed, mangled, and disfigured. He was clearly badly hurt.

"Dear God!" the coachman wailed. "What more could I have done? If I had been driving fast, or if I had not shouted at him -- but I was going slowly, not in any hurry. Everyone could see I was driving like everyone else. A drunk cannot walk straight -- we all know that.... I saw him crossing the street, staggering, nearly falling. I shouted again, a second time, a third time, then I reined the horses in, but he fell right under their hooves! Either he did it on purpose or he was too far gone.... The horses are young, easily spooked... they bolted, he screamed... that made it worse. That is how it happened!"
"That is exactly how it was," a voice in the crowd confirmed.
"He shouted, it is true -- he shouted three times," said another voice.
"Three times exactly -- we all heard it," a third voice called out.

But the coachman was not especially distressed or frightened. The carriage clearly belonged to a rich, important person who was waiting for it somewhere. The police were naturally anxious not to upset his plans. All they had to do was get the injured man to the police station and the hospital. No one knew his name.
Meanwhile Raskolnikov had squeezed through and bent closer over him. The lantern suddenly lit up the victim's face. He recognized him.

"I know him! I know him!" he shouted, pushing to the front. "He is a retired government clerk -- Marmeladov. He lives nearby, in Kozel's building.... Get a doctor! I will pay -- look!" He pulled money from his pocket and showed it to the policeman. He was in a state of violent agitation.

The police were glad to learn who the man was. Raskolnikov gave his own name and address, and as earnestly as though it were his own father, he begged the police to carry the unconscious Marmeladov to his lodgings immediately.

"Right here -- three houses away," he said eagerly. "The building belongs to Kozel, a rich German. He was on his way home, no doubt drunk. I know him -- he is a drunkard. He has a family there -- a wife, children. He has a daughter.... It will take too long to get him to the hospital, and there must be a doctor somewhere in the building. I will pay, I will pay! At least he will be looked after at home... they can help him right away. But he will die before you get him to the hospital." He managed to slip something unseen into the policeman's hand. But the matter was straightforward and legitimate, and in any case help was closer here. They lifted the injured man, and people volunteered to carry him.
Kozel's building was thirty yards away. Raskolnikov walked behind, carefully supporting Marmeladov's head and showing the way.
"This way, this way! Head first going up the stairs. Turn him around! I will pay -- I will make it worth your while," he murmured.

Katerina Ivanovna had been doing what she always did in her free moments -- pacing back and forth in her little room from the window to the stove and back, arms folded across her chest, talking to herself and coughing. Lately she had taken to talking more than ever to her eldest daughter, Polenka, a girl of ten, who understood much less than she grasped but knew very well that her mother needed her, and so always watched her with wide, knowing eyes and tried her hardest to look like she understood. This time Polenka was undressing her little brother, who had been sick all day and was going to bed. The boy was waiting for her to take off his shirt, which had to be washed overnight. He sat perfectly still on a chair -- silent, serious, legs straight out in front of him, heels together, toes pointing out.

He was listening to what his mother was telling his sister, sitting motionless with pursed lips and big round eyes -- exactly the way all good little boys are supposed to sit when being undressed for bed. A still younger girl, dressed literally in rags, stood behind the screen waiting her turn. The door to the stairway was open to provide some relief from the clouds of tobacco smoke that drifted in from the other rooms and sent the poor consumptive woman into long, terrible fits of coughing. Katerina Ivanovna seemed to have grown even thinner that week, and the hectic flush on her cheeks was brighter than ever.

"You would not believe, you cannot imagine, Polenka," she said, pacing the room, "what a happy, luxurious life we had in my papa's house, and how this drunkard has brought me to ruin -- and will bring all of you to ruin! Papa was a civil colonel, only a step away from governor. Everyone who visited him said, 'We regard you, Ivan Mihailovitch, as our governor!' When I... when..." she coughed violently, "oh, this cursed life!" she cried, pressing her hands to her chest. "When at my last ball... at the marshal's... Princess Bezzemelny saw me -- the same one who blessed me when your father and I married, Polenka -- she immediately asked: 'Is that not the lovely girl who danced the shawl dance at the graduation ceremony?' (You must mend that tear -- take your needle and darn it the way I showed you, or tomorrow" -- cough, cough, cough -- "he will make the hole bigger," she forced out.) "Prince Schegolskoy, a kammerjunker just arrived from Petersburg... danced the mazurka with me and wanted to propose the next day. But I thanked him with the most flattering expressions and told him my heart had long belonged to another. That other was your father, Polya. Papa was furious.... Is the water ready? Give me the shirt, and the stockings! Lida," she called to the youngest, "you will have to sleep without your chemise tonight... lay your stockings out with it... I will wash them together.... Why does that drunken vagabond not come home? He has worn his shirt until it looks like a dishrag, torn it to shreds! I would do it all together so I would not have to work two nights in a row! Oh, God!" (Cough, cough, cough, cough!) "Again! What is this?" she cried, noticing a crowd in the hallway and men pushing into her room with a burden. "What is it? What are they carrying? Have mercy!"
"Where should we put him?" the policeman asked, looking around after Marmeladov, unconscious and covered in blood, had been carried in.
"On the sofa! Lay him right on the sofa, with his head this way," Raskolnikov directed.
"Run over in the street! Drunk!" someone shouted in the hallway.
Katerina Ivanovna stood frozen, turning white and gasping for breath. The children were terrified. Little Lida screamed, rushed to Polenka, and clung to her, trembling all over.
As soon as they had laid Marmeladov down, Raskolnikov rushed to Katerina Ivanovna.

"For God's sake, stay calm, do not be frightened!" he said quickly. "He was crossing the street and a carriage hit him. Do not be frightened, he will come to. I told them to bring him here... I have been here before, you remember? He will come to. I will pay!"
"This time he has done it!" Katerina Ivanovna cried in despair and rushed to her husband.

Raskolnikov noticed immediately that she was not the kind of woman who faints easily. In an instant she placed a pillow under the unfortunate man's head -- something no one else had thought of -- and began undressing and examining him. She kept her wits about her, forgetting herself, biting her trembling lips and stifling the screams rising in her throat.
Meanwhile, Raskolnikov persuaded someone to run for a doctor. It turned out there was one two doors down.

"I have sent for a doctor," he kept assuring Katerina Ivanovna. "Do not worry, I will pay. Is there water?... And give me a napkin or a towel, anything, quickly.... He is injured but not dead, believe me.... We will see what the doctor says!"

Katerina Ivanovna ran to the window. There, on a broken chair in the corner, a large earthenware basin full of water had been set out, ready for washing the children's and her husband's clothes that night. Katerina Ivanovna did this washing at night at least twice a week, sometimes more. The family had reached such a state that they had practically no change of clothes, and Katerina Ivanovna could not stand uncleanliness. Rather than see dirt in the house, she preferred to work herself to exhaustion at night while everyone slept, hanging the wet clothes on a line to be dry by morning. She picked up the basin at Raskolnikov's request but nearly fell under its weight. But Raskolnikov had already found a towel, wetted it, and begun washing the blood from Marmeladov's face.

Katerina Ivanovna stood nearby, breathing painfully, pressing her hands to her chest. She needed help herself. Raskolnikov was beginning to realize he might have made a mistake in having the injured man brought here. The policeman stood there looking uncertain too.

"Polenka!" Katerina Ivanovna called out. "Run to Sonia -- quickly. If she is not home, leave word that her father has been run over and she must come here at once... as soon as she gets back. Run, Polenka! Here -- put on the shawl."
"Run as fast as you can!" the little boy on the chair cried out suddenly, after which he sank back into the same mute rigidity -- round eyes, heels thrust forward, toes spread apart.

Meanwhile the room had filled with so many people you could not have dropped a pin. The policemen left, all except one who stayed for a while trying to shoo back the crowd pressing in from the stairway. Nearly all of Madame Lippevechsel's lodgers had streamed in from the inner rooms -- first they were packed in the doorway, then they overflowed into the room. Katerina Ivanovna was furious.

"Can you not at least let him die in peace!" she shouted at the crowd. "Is this a show for your entertainment? With your cigarettes!" (Cough, cough, cough!) "You might as well keep your hats on!... And there is one wearing his! Get out! Have some respect for the dead, at least!"

The coughing choked her, but her rebukes had some effect. They clearly had a certain fear of Katerina Ivanovna. The lodgers, one by one, squeezed back into the doorway with that peculiar inner satisfaction that can always be observed among bystanders at a sudden disaster -- a feeling that no living person is exempt from, even among those closest to the victim, and regardless of how sincere their sympathy and compassion may be.
Voices in the hallway could be heard, though, saying the man should be taken to the hospital and that people had no business creating a disturbance here.

"No business dying!" Katerina Ivanovna cried, and she was rushing to the door to unleash her fury on them when she came face to face in the doorway with Madame Lippevechsel, who had only just heard about the accident and had come to restore order. She was an especially quarrelsome and unreasonable German.
"Oh, my God!" she cried, wringing her hands. "Your husband, drunken horses have trampled! To the hospital with him! I am the landlady!"

"Amalia Ludwigovna, I beg you to consider what you are saying," Katerina Ivanovna began in a haughty tone -- she always took a haughty tone with the landlady so that the woman would "remember her place," and even now she could not deny herself this satisfaction. "Amalia Ludwigovna..."
"I have told you once before that you may not dare call me Amalia Ludwigovna. I am Amalia Ivanovna."

"You are not Amalia Ivanovna but Amalia Ludwigovna, and since I am not one of your contemptible flatterers like Mr. Lebeziatnikov, who is laughing behind the door at this very moment" -- indeed, a laugh and the words "they are at it again" were audible from the doorway -- "I shall always call you Amalia Ludwigovna, though I cannot fathom why you dislike the name. You can see for yourself what has happened to Semyon Zaharovitch. He is dying. I ask you to close that door immediately and let no one in. Let him at least die in peace! Otherwise, I promise you, the Governor-General himself will be informed of your behavior tomorrow. The prince knew me as a girl; he remembers Semyon Zaharovitch well and has often been a benefactor to him. Everyone knows Semyon Zaharovitch had many friends and patrons whom he gave up himself, out of honorable pride, knowing his unfortunate weakness. But now" -- she pointed at Raskolnikov -- "a generous young man with means and connections, whom Semyon Zaharovitch has known since childhood, has come to our aid. You may rest assured, Amalia Ludwigovna..."

All this was delivered with extreme rapidity, getting faster and faster, but a coughing fit suddenly cut Katerina Ivanovna short. At that instant the dying man regained consciousness and groaned. She ran to him. The injured man opened his eyes and, without recognition or understanding, stared at Raskolnikov bending over him. He drew deep, slow, painful breaths. Blood seeped from the corners of his mouth and sweat beaded on his forehead. Not recognizing Raskolnikov, he began looking around anxiously. Katerina Ivanovna gazed at him with a sad but stern expression. Tears trickled from her eyes.
"My God! His whole chest is crushed! Look at the blood," she said in despair. "We must get his clothes off. Turn a little, Semyon Zaharovitch, if you can," she called to him.
Marmeladov recognized her.
"A priest," he said hoarsely.
Katerina Ivanovna went to the window, leaned her head against the frame, and cried out in despair:
"Oh, this cursed life!"
"A priest," the dying man said again after a moment's silence.

"They have gone for one!" Katerina Ivanovna shouted. He obeyed her shout and fell silent. With sad, timid eyes he searched for her. She came back and stood by his pillow. He seemed slightly easier, but not for long.
Soon his eyes found little Lida, his favorite, who was shaking in the corner as though having a fit, staring at him with her wide, wondering child's eyes.
"A-ah," he gestured toward her anxiously. He wanted to say something.
"What now?" cried Katerina Ivanovna.
"Barefoot, barefoot!" he muttered, pointing with frantic eyes at the child's bare feet.
"Be quiet," Katerina Ivanovna snapped. "You know perfectly well why she is barefoot."
"Thank God -- the doctor!" Raskolnikov exclaimed with relief.

The doctor came in -- a precise little old man, a German, who looked around mistrustfully. He went up to the sick man, took his pulse, and carefully felt his head. Then, with Katerina Ivanovna's help, he unbuttoned the blood-soaked shirt and exposed the injured man's chest. It was gashed, crushed, and fractured -- several ribs on the right side were broken. On the left, just over the heart, was a large, sinister yellowish-black bruise from a savage kick of the horse's hoof. The doctor frowned. The policeman told him the man had been caught in the wheel and dragged about thirty yards along the road.
"It is remarkable that he regained consciousness at all," the doctor whispered softly to Raskolnikov.
"What do you think?" Raskolnikov asked.
"He will die any minute."
"Is there really no hope?"
"Not the slightest. He is at the very end.... His head is badly injured too.... Hmm... I could bleed him, if you like, but... it would be pointless. He will be dead within five or ten minutes."
"Then bleed him."
"If you wish.... But I warn you it will be perfectly useless."

At that moment more footsteps were heard. The crowd in the hallway parted, and the priest -- a small, grey old man -- appeared in the doorway carrying the sacrament. A policeman had gone for him at the time of the accident. The doctor stepped aside, exchanging glances with him. Raskolnikov asked the doctor to stay a bit longer. He shrugged but remained.

Everyone stepped back. The confession was brief. The dying man probably understood very little; he could only produce broken, indistinct sounds. Katerina Ivanovna took little Lida, lifted the boy from his chair, and knelt in the corner by the stove, making the children kneel before her. The little girl was still trembling, but the boy, kneeling on his small bare knees, rhythmically raised his hand, crossed himself with precision, and bowed down until his forehead touched the floor -- a gesture that seemed to give him particular satisfaction. Katerina Ivanovna bit her lips and held back her tears. She prayed too, occasionally straightening the boy's shirt and managing to drape a kerchief from the chest over the girl's bare shoulders -- all without rising from her knees or pausing in her prayer. Meanwhile the door from the inner rooms cracked open again. In the hallway, the crowd of spectators from every apartment on the staircase grew denser, though no one dared cross the threshold. A single candle stub lit the scene.

At that moment Polenka forced her way through the crowd. She came in breathless from running, pulled off her kerchief, found her mother, went up to her, and said: "She is coming. I met her in the street." Her mother made her kneel beside her.

Timidly and noiselessly, a young girl made her way through the crowd, and her appearance in that room -- amid the poverty, the rags, the death and despair -- was startling. She too was in rags, cheap clothes, but decked out in the garish, unmistakable finery of the streets. Sonia stopped in the doorway and looked around, bewildered, seeming unconscious of everything. She had forgotten her secondhand, gaudy silk dress, so inappropriate here with its absurd long train, and her enormous crinoline that filled the whole doorway, and her light-colored shoes, and the parasol she had brought along though it was useless at night, and her ridiculous round straw hat with its blazing flame-colored feather. Under this rakishly tilted hat was a pale, frightened little face with parted lips and eyes wide with terror. Sonia was a small, thin girl of eighteen with fair hair, rather pretty, with remarkable blue eyes. She stared at the bed and the priest. She too was out of breath from running. At last whispers and a few words from the crowd probably reached her. She looked down and took a step into the room, still staying close to the door.
The service was over. Katerina Ivanovna went back to her husband. The priest stepped aside and turned to offer a few words of consolation to Katerina Ivanovna before leaving.
"And what am I supposed to do with these?" she interrupted sharply and irritably, pointing at the children.
"God is merciful. Look to the Almighty for help," the priest began.
"Ha! He is merciful -- but not to us."
"That is a sin, madam," the priest said, shaking his head.
"And is _that_ not a sin?" cried Katerina Ivanovna, pointing at the dying man.
"Perhaps those who inadvertently caused the accident will agree to compensate you, at least for the loss of his income."

"You do not understand!" Katerina Ivanovna cried angrily, waving her hand. "Why should they compensate me? He was drunk and threw himself under the horses! What income? He brought us nothing but misery. He drank everything away, the drunkard! He robbed us to pay for his drinking, he wasted their lives and mine on drink! And thank God he is dying! One less mouth to feed!"
"You must forgive in the hour of death. Such feelings are a grave sin, madam."

Katerina Ivanovna was busy with the dying man -- giving him water, wiping the blood and sweat from his face, straightening his pillow. She had only turned to speak to the priest for a moment. Now she flew at him almost in a frenzy.

"Oh, Father! Those are just words! Forgive! If he had not been run over, he would have come home tonight drunk, with his only shirt filthy and in rags, and collapsed like a log. And I would have spent the whole night scrubbing and rinsing, washing his rags and the children's, then drying them by the window -- and at daybreak I would have been darning them. That is how I spend my nights!... What is the point of talking about forgiveness? I have already forgiven!"

A terrible, hollow cough cut her short. She pressed a handkerchief to her lips and showed it to the priest, clutching her aching chest with her other hand. The handkerchief was soaked with blood. The priest bowed his head and said nothing.

Marmeladov was in his death agony. He did not take his eyes off Katerina Ivanovna's face as she bent over him again. He kept trying to say something, moving his tongue with difficulty and forming indistinct words. But Katerina Ivanovna, understanding that he wanted to beg forgiveness, cut him off:
"Quiet! No need! I know what you want to say!" And the dying man fell silent. But at that same moment his wandering eyes found the doorway, and he saw Sonia.
Until then he had not noticed her. She was standing in the shadows, in a corner.
"Who is that? Who is that?" he said suddenly, in a thick, gasping voice, in agitation, turning his horrified eyes toward the door where his daughter stood, and struggling to sit up.
"Lie down! Lie _down_!" cried Katerina Ivanovna.

With unnatural strength he had managed to prop himself on his elbow. He stared wildly and fixedly at his daughter for some time, as though not recognizing her. He had never seen her dressed like this before. Suddenly he recognized her -- crushed, ashamed, standing there in her humiliation and garish finery, meekly waiting her turn to say goodbye to her dying father. His face showed intense suffering.

"Sonia! Daughter! Forgive!" he cried, and he tried to reach out to her, but losing his balance, he tumbled off the sofa face-first onto the floor. They rushed to pick him up and put him back, but he was dying. Sonia, with a faint cry, ran to him, threw her arms around him, and held him. He died in her embrace.
"He got what he wanted," Katerina Ivanovna cried, seeing her husband's body. "Well, what now? How am I supposed to bury him? And what will I feed them tomorrow?"
Raskolnikov went up to Katerina Ivanovna.

"Katerina Ivanovna," he began, "last week your husband told me the entire story of his life and circumstances.... Believe me, he spoke of you with passionate reverence. From that evening, when I learned how devoted he was to all of you, and how he loved and respected you especially, Katerina Ivanovna, despite his unfortunate weakness -- from that evening we became friends.... Allow me now... to do something... to repay my debt to my dead friend. Here are twenty rubles -- if that can help at all, then... I... in short, I will come again, I will definitely come again... I may even come tomorrow.... Goodbye!"

And he hurried out of the room, pushing through the crowd to the stairs. But in the crowd he suddenly bumped into Nikodim Fomitch, who had heard about the accident and come to give instructions personally. They had not met since the scene at the police station, but Nikodim Fomitch recognized him instantly.
"Ah, is that you?" he asked.

"He is dead," Raskolnikov answered. "The doctor and the priest have been -- everything was done properly. Do not upset the poor woman too much -- she has consumption as it is. Try to cheer her up if you can... you are a kind man, I know..." he added with a smile, looking straight into his face.
"But you are spattered with blood," Nikodim Fomitch remarked, noticing in the lamplight some fresh stains on Raskolnikov's waistcoat.
"Yes... I am covered in blood," Raskolnikov said with a peculiar expression, then smiled, nodded, and headed downstairs.

He descended slowly and deliberately, feverish but unaware of it, entirely consumed by a new, overwhelming sensation of life and strength that had suddenly surged up within him. This feeling was like that of a condemned man who has just been pardoned. Halfway down the stairs, the priest overtook him on his way home. Raskolnikov let him pass with a silent nod. But as he was descending the final steps, he heard hurried footsteps behind him. Someone was chasing him. It was Polenka. She was running after him, calling: "Wait! Wait!"

He turned around. She was at the bottom of the staircase, stopped one step above him. Dim light came in from the courtyard. Raskolnikov could make out the child's thin but pretty little face, looking at him with a bright, childish smile. She had run after him with a message she was obviously delighted to deliver.
"Tell me, what is your name?... And where do you live?" she asked breathlessly, in a rapid voice.
He placed both hands on her shoulders and looked at her with something like rapture. It gave him such joy to look at her -- he could not have said why.
"Who sent you?"
"Sister Sonia sent me," the girl answered, smiling even more brightly.
"I knew it was Sister Sonia who sent you."
"Mama sent me too... when Sister Sonia was sending me, Mama came over too and said: 'Run fast, Polenka.'"
"Do you love Sister Sonia?"
"I love her more than anyone," Polenka answered with a special earnestness, and her smile grew more serious.
"And will you love me?"

By way of answer, he saw the little girl's face drawing near, her full lips innocently held out to kiss him. Then her thin, stick-like arms held him tightly, her head rested on his shoulder, and she wept softly, pressing her face against him.

"I feel sorry for Papa," she said after a moment, lifting her tear-streaked face and wiping her eyes with her hands. "It is nothing but bad luck now," she added suddenly with the peculiarly solemn air children put on when they are trying to talk like adults.
"Did your father love you?"

"He loved Lida most," she went on very seriously, without smiling, exactly like a grown-up. "He loved her because she is little and because she is sick. And he always used to bring her presents. But he taught us to read, and me grammar and scripture too," she added with dignity. "And Mama never said anything, but we knew she was pleased, and Papa knew it too. And Mama wants to teach me French, because it is time my education began."
"And do you know your prayers?"

"Of course we do! We have known them for a long time. I say mine silently because I am a big girl now, but Kolya and Lida say theirs aloud with Mama. First they say the Hail Mary, and then another prayer: 'Lord, forgive and bless Sister Sonia,' and then: 'Lord, forgive and bless our second father.' Our first father is dead, and this is the other one, but we pray for the first one too."
"Polenka, my name is Rodion. Pray for me too sometimes. 'And Thy servant Rodion' -- nothing more."
"I will pray for you for the rest of my life," the little girl declared passionately, and suddenly smiling again, she threw herself at him and hugged him tightly once more.

Raskolnikov told her his name and address and promised to come the next day without fail. The child went away completely enchanted with him. It was past ten when he stepped into the street. Five minutes later he was standing on the bridge, at the exact spot where the woman had jumped in.

"Enough," he declared, resolutely and triumphantly. "I am done with delusions, imaginary terrors, and phantoms! Life is real! Have I not just lived? My life did not die with that old woman! May the Kingdom of Heaven be hers -- and now enough, old woman, your time is up! Now begins the reign of reason and light... and of will, and of strength... and now we shall see! We shall test our strength!" he added defiantly, as though challenging some invisible power. "And I was ready to accept living on a square yard of space!

"I am very weak right now, but... I believe my illness is over. I knew it would pass when I went out. By the way, Potchinkov's building is just a few steps from here. I should definitely go to Razumihin, even if it were not nearby... let him win his bet! Let us give him some satisfaction too -- it does not matter! Strength -- strength is what you need. You cannot get anything without it, and strength must be won by strength -- that is what they do not understand," he added, proudly and self-assuredly. He walked from the bridge with faltering steps. Pride and self-confidence grew steadily stronger in him. He was becoming a different man with every passing moment. What had happened to work this transformation? He did not know himself. Like a man grasping at a straw, he suddenly felt that he too "could live, that there was still life left for him, that his life had not died with the old woman." Perhaps he was jumping to conclusions too quickly, but he did not stop to think about that.
"But I did ask her to pray for 'Thy servant Rodion,'" the thought struck him. "Well, that was... just in case," he added, and laughed at his own boyish joke. He was in excellent spirits.

He found Razumihin easily. The new tenant was already known at Potchinkov's, and the building manager showed him the way at once. Halfway up the stairs he could hear the noise and animated conversation of a large gathering. The door to the stairway was wide open. He could hear shouts and debate. Razumihin's room was fairly large, and the company numbered about fifteen people. Raskolnikov stopped in the entry, where two of the landlady's servants were busy behind a screen with samovars, bottles, plates, and dishes of pie and snacks brought up from the landlady's kitchen. Raskolnikov sent word in for Razumihin. He came running out, delighted. It was immediately obvious that he had drunk a great deal. Though no amount of liquor could truly make Razumihin drunk, this time the effects were visible.

"Listen," Raskolnikov said quickly, "I only came to tell you that you have won your bet and that no one really knows what may happen to them. I cannot come in -- I am so weak I will fall down any second. So good evening and goodbye! Come see me tomorrow."
"You know what? I will walk you home. If you say you are that weak, you need--"
"And your guests? Who is the curly-haired one who just peeked out?"

"Him? God only knows! Some friend of my uncle's, I expect, or maybe he showed up uninvited... I will leave my uncle with them -- he is an invaluable man. Too bad I cannot introduce you right now. But forget them all! They will not even notice I am gone, and I need some fresh air anyway. You came at just the right moment -- another two minutes and I would have started a fight! They are spouting such insane nonsense... you cannot imagine what people will say! Though actually, why not? Do we not talk nonsense ourselves? And let them... that is how you learn not to!... Wait -- let me get Zossimov."
Zossimov pounced on Raskolnikov almost eagerly and showed a particular interest in him. Soon his face brightened.
"You need to go straight to bed," he said after examining the patient as best he could, "and take something for the night. Will you? I prepared it earlier... a powder."
"Two, if you like," Raskolnikov answered. He took the powder immediately.
"Good that you are seeing him home," Zossimov said to Razumihin. "We will see how he is tomorrow. He is not bad today -- a considerable improvement since this afternoon. Live and learn..."

"Do you know what Zossimov whispered to me as we left?" Razumihin burst out as soon as they were in the street. "I will not tell you everything, brother, because they are such fools. Zossimov told me to talk freely with you on the way and get you to talk freely to me, and afterward I am to report back to him, because he has gotten it into his head that you are... mad, or close to it. Can you imagine! First, you have three times his brains. Second, if you are not mad, you could not care less about his wild theory. And third, that slab of meat whose specialty is surgery has gone off on a tangent about mental illness. And what brought him to this conclusion about you was your conversation today with Zametov."
"Zametov told you everything?"

"Yes, and he was right to. Now I understand it all, and so does Zametov.... The thing is, Rodya... the point is... I am a bit drunk now.... But never mind... the point is that this idea... you understand? was just beginning to hatch in their minds... you understand? That is, nobody dared say it out loud, because the idea is too absurd -- especially since they arrested that painter, the whole thing burst like a bubble. But why are they such fools? I gave Zametov a bit of a beating at the time -- that is between us, brother, do not let on that you know. I have noticed he is touchy about it. It was at Luise Ivanovna's. But today -- today it has all been cleared up. It is mainly that Ilya Petrovitch's doing! He took advantage of your fainting at the station, though he is ashamed of it himself now. I know that for a fact..."
Raskolnikov listened greedily. Razumihin was drunk enough to talk too freely.
"I fainted because it was stuffy and the paint fumes," Raskolnikov said.

"No need to explain that! And it was not just the paint -- the fever had been building for a month. Zossimov will vouch for that! But you should see how crushed that boy Zametov is now -- you would not believe it! 'I am not worth his little finger,' he says. Yours, he means. He has his good moments, brother. But the lesson you gave him today at the Palais de Cristal -- that was priceless! You terrified him at first, you know -- he nearly had convulsions! You practically had him believing all that horrible nonsense again, and then you just -- stuck your tongue out at him! 'There, what do you make of that?' Perfect! He is crushed, destroyed! It was masterful, I swear! Exactly what they deserve! Too bad I was not there! He was hoping to see you desperately. Porfiry wants to meet you too..."
"Ah!... him too... but why did they brand me a madman?"

"Not exactly mad. I must have said too much, brother.... What struck him, you see, was that you seemed interested only in that one subject. Now it is clear why it interested you -- knowing all the circumstances... and how it agitated you and got tangled up with your illness... I am a bit drunk, brother, but to hell with him -- he has some theory of his own... I am telling you, he is obsessed with mental illness. But do not let it bother you..."
For half a minute neither spoke.

"Listen, Razumihin," Raskolnikov began, "I want to tell you something plainly. I have just been at a deathbed -- a clerk who died... I gave them all my money... and besides, I was just kissed by someone who, if I had killed anyone, would still... I mean, I also saw someone else there... with a flame-colored feather... but I am rambling. I am very weak -- hold me up... the stairs are right here..."
"What is it? What is the matter?" Razumihin asked anxiously.
"I am a bit dizzy, but that is not the point. I am so sad, so sad... like a woman. Look -- what is that? Look, look!"
"What?"
"Do you not see? There is a light in my room -- see? Through the crack..."
They were already at the foot of the last flight of stairs, on the level of the landlady's door, and from there they could indeed see that a light was burning in Raskolnikov's garret.
"Strange! Nastasya, perhaps," Razumihin suggested.
"She is never in my room at this hour. She must be in bed by now, but... I do not care! Goodbye!"
"What do you mean? I am coming in with you! We will go in together!"
"I know we are going in together, but I want to shake your hand here and say goodbye to you here. So give me your hand -- goodbye!"
"What is wrong with you, Rodya?"
"Nothing... come on... you will be my witness."
They started up the stairs, and the thought crossed Razumihin's mind that perhaps Zossimov was right after all. "I must have upset him with my chattering!" he muttered to himself.
When they reached the door, they heard voices inside the room.
"What is going on?" cried Razumihin. Raskolnikov was the first to open the door. He flung it wide and stood frozen in the doorway.

His mother and sister were sitting on his sofa, and they had been waiting for an hour and a half. Why had he never expected them, never imagined they might be here -- even though the news of their departure, their journey, their imminent arrival had been told to him repeatedly, just that day? They had spent that hour and a half questioning Nastasya, who stood before them now and had already told them everything. They had been beside themselves with alarm when they learned he had "run off" that day while ill and, as they gathered from Nastasya, delirious. Good God, what had become of him? Both had been weeping, both had been in anguish for that hour and a half.

A cry of joy and ecstasy greeted Raskolnikov's entrance. Both women rushed to him. But he stood like a dead man. A sudden, unbearable sensation struck him like a thunderbolt. He could not lift his arms to embrace them. He could not. His mother and sister hugged him, kissed him, laughed, and wept. He took a step, swayed, and collapsed, unconscious.
Panic, cries of horror, moans... Razumihin, who had been standing in the doorway, flew into the room, scooped up the sick man in his powerful arms, and had him on the sofa in an instant.

"It is nothing, nothing!" he cried to the mother and sister. "It is just a faint, a trifle! The doctor said just now that he is much better, that he is perfectly well! Water! Look -- he is already coming around. It is all right now!"

And seizing Dounia by the arm so hard he nearly dislocated it, he made her lean down to see that "he is all right now." The mother and sister looked at Razumihin with emotion and gratitude, as though he were their guardian angel. They had already heard from Nastasya everything this "very capable young man," as Pulcheria Alexandrovna called him that evening in conversation with Dounia, had done for their Rodya during his illness.
